Jurisdiction: small island territory under a wider kingdom's framework. Same-sex marriage legal since 2024 (via supreme court ruling of parent state), partnerships 2016, anti-discrimination in criminal code covering sexual orientation only (not gender identity). No trans-specific provision, no documented trans-specific violence, no documented legal gender recognition. Tourism board markets as LGBT destination. Local equality org: "It has always been accepting, as long as it's not in their face. People are out, but discreetly out. There has never been anything official." Religious influence main brake. 2015 intergovernmental endorsement of equal rights for LGBT persons expressly including transgender persons; territory's rep acknowledged conservative norms made coming out difficult for LGBT youth, stigmatised as disordered. Harassment documented 2004-2007 (rocks thrown at lesbian couple), no later instance.

So: no criminalisation of trans identity; no trans-specific criminal law. No state threat-framing of a tier-1 kind (no facility bans, no custody rules documented). No documented police targeting of trans people. No documented trans-specific violence. Social climate: tolerant but discreet, "not in their face" — social friction; conservative norms, youth stigma. That's friction (a) with some elements of (b) social hostility? "not in their face" implies disapproval if visible — mild.

No trans-specific protections: anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation only. So no recourse for anti-trans discrimination documented. Missing: legal gender recognition (resident gap, not visitor exposure — explicitly don't deduct). Documents: visitor uses home passport; no documented border friction for trans visitors. Uncertainty: whether officials would doubt foreign documents — undocumented, and per rule 13 an open question is lighter than a known good.

Other agents: no documented trans-specific violence; the only harassment record is dated 2004-2007, which is weak evidence about present in either direction.

Positive signals: stable, functioning rule of law; institutional acceptance trend (marriage 2024, partnerships 2016, intergovernmental endorsement including transgender persons). Social acceptance: tourism, LGBT venues, equality orgs, "tolerant and mostly open". Thin formal recourse for trans specifically (no GI in anti-discrimination grounds), no data on police response to trans victims.

Where does this sit? Compared with anchors: severe risk is far; 0.35 anchors involve hostile state machinery (visitor registers, police stops, forced eviction, monitored travel). None documented here. 0.55 anchors: 0.55-A registration with police and checkpoints, discretionary holds; 0.55-B border secondary screening; 0.55-C hospital ward by document sex; but here no documented administrative registration/checkpoint, no documented document screening, and no facility rule documented. Hmm — 0.55-C is about ward assignment by ID marker; here no such rule documented; cannot infer.

0.65 anchors: documented incidents with functioning remedies and national equality law protecting gender identity — some more than here. Here there's no GI protection, but also no documented incident. 0.75 anchors: protections operating (health charter, transit ombudsman, tribunal). Here there's no documented trans-specific protection machinery.

0.85 anchors: explicit gender identity protections and working remedies — clearly above this dossier.

So the dossier has: no documented traveler-facing exposure at all (no border friction, no criminalisation, no facility bans, no police targeting, no violence). But also no documented trans-specific protection or remedy; and documentary silence on gender identity. Social climate: "accepting as long as not in their face" — friction, mild hostility toward visible nonconformity.

Per rule 3 and 13: known goods — a functioning rule of law state, LGBT-tolerant society, no criminalisation, official endorsement of trans rights, LGBT venues. Absent: trans-specific protections, so if a trans visitor is harassed, the anti-discrimination statute doesn't cover them; but generic assault/harassment law presumably applies (not documented though).

Also relevant: this is a small island — one incident carries statistical weight; but the single documented incident is 20 years old and involves a lesbian couple during a legal challenge, not a trans visitor.

I'd place this around 0.62–0.70. It has strong acceptance signals but no trans-specific protection and a "discreetly out" social climate with a stigma-of-disorder history for LGBT youth (2015 acknowledgment). Given the absence of any documented exposure and the presence of documented social tolerance and legal functioning, but thin trans-specific recourse — I'd say 0.65. That's in the Reduced Risk band, similar to the 0.65 anchors which had documented incidents but with remedies and equality law covering gender identity. Here there's no documented incident, so arguably better; but no GI protection. Hmm.

Compare with 0.65-B (Tambera): health law guarantees care and ombudsperson overturned refusal — documented protection working, but repeated misgendering. That's a working protection. Here we have no working trans-specific protection documented. However, the 0.65 anchors all had documented incidents and the jurisdiction had explicit GI protections. Their score 0.65 reflects asymmetric: protections exist but inconsistently enforced. Here: no protections but no incidents.

Rubric: "no criminalisation" is not a floor; a jurisdiction with documented universal-exposure practices or discrimination prevalence at scale without working remedy sits in Elevated Risk. Here neither is documented — no universal-exposure practices documented, no discrimination prevalence at scale. So it doesn't fall into Elevated. The absence of GI protection is a resident-facing gap (their criminal code's enumerated grounds) — not a visitor exposure per se, though it signals no remedy for trans-specific discrimination. That's a "resident gap" — rule 1 says don't deduct for missing domestic machinery unless it reaches visitors. Anti-discrimination protection coverage is arguably a climate signal.

So: no documented exposures, documented climate signals positive (functioning rule of law, LGBT destination, official endorsement of trans rights, no criminalisation), some friction ("not in their face", youth stigma as disordered). That points to Reduced Risk, maybe 0.68–0.72.

I'll pick 0.68. Hmm, or 0.65. That's documented protections operating. Here we have no documented border practice — open question. Lower than 0.75. Compared to 0.65 anchors: documented protections plus documented incidents with remedies. Here we have an undocumented set of protections. Rule 13: "a latent tangential statute plus open questions plus thin formal recourse hold the jurisdiction a step below the acceptance-with-protections tier — a step, not a tier." Here there is no latent statute at all (no trans offence, no same-sex offence). But there are open questions (border, documents) and thin formal recourse (no GI in anti-discrimination) plus documented social acceptance. So a step below the acceptance-with-protections tier (0.85 tier) → 0.65-0.70. I'll go 0.68.
